sents: Today’s AI is mostly trained in a similar manner: when the AI gives a reply, a scoring agent working from a rubric considers whether it is helpful to the user.
Does it make the user more likely to accept it?
Which is whether the user will be happy.
And even when humans score the replies themselves, every turn they evaluate whether they are happy with the result.
As emergent behaviour, this may lead to the outcome the human needed.
And it’s very easy for AI to lose sight of what the user wants to achieve in the long run, over the whole conversation.
Having talked much about how turn-based training falls short in achieving real-life goals, I do not mean to say that relying on emergent behaviour is not the way to achieve general intelligence.
In fact, for a large part of human education, children were graded on micro-improvements one step at a time, similar to the turn-based method used to train AI.

The idea is that the student who always had As in primary school will probably always have As in high school, will probably also have a lot of As in university, and will achieve a lot in their lifetime.
And very often it is the case.
Many of the best lawyers and doctors have been A students since they started school.
However, there are two big differences.

The intended reader has read the essay's introduction, which lists seven pillars, the behaviours an AI employee needs; this chapter is about the first of them, and the text below comes from later in that chapter.

The text, each paragraph starting with its number:

[P1] Today’s AI is mostly trained in a similar manner: when the AI gives a reply, a scoring agent working from a rubric considers whether it is helpful to the user. Does it make the user more likely to accept it? Which is whether the user will be happy. And even when humans score the replies themselves, every turn they evaluate whether they are happy with the result. As emergent behaviour, this may lead to the outcome the human needed. But it is a struggle. And it’s very easy for AI to lose sight of what the user wants to achieve in the long run, over the whole conversation.

[P2] Having talked much about how turn-based training falls short in achieving real-life goals, I do not mean to say that relying on emergent behaviour is not the way to achieve general intelligence. In fact, for a large part of human education, children were graded on micro-improvements one step at a time, similar to the turn-based method used to train AI. The idea is that the student who always had As in primary school will probably always have As in high school, will probably also have a lot of As in university, and will achieve a lot in their lifetime. And very often it is the case. Many of the best lawyers and doctors have been A students since they started school. However, there are two big differences.

Score each sentence on the offence below. A score is roughly how many intended readers in ten would meet the problem at that sentence (0 = none, 9 = nearly all).

1. Unmarked turn: for a sentence that turns from stating a point to illustrating it with a generic person, company or scene, score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to want words that mark the turn, such as "Consider…", "Take…" or "For example…".

Spelling and grammar do not count.
